Explanation

Your application is trying to reach external resources via HTTP protocol.

For Managed Instance on App Service, secure connectivity to internal/on-prem HTTP services is managed via plan-level VNet integration and private endpoints. Keep inbound traffic restricted to 80/443; capture any required HTTP config in install scripts. Use Bastion JIT RDP only for diagnostics—persist all changes via install scripts. Outbound traffic does not impose similar restrictions.

While if targeting other Azure compute services, ensure the resources it is trying to reach are accessible from the Azure environment. If those HTTP requests are sent to internal services or services hosted on-prem, you probably will need to migrate those services to Azure as well.

Also, keep in mind that Azure App Service supports port 80 for HTTP and port 443 for HTTPS traffic. If you are using any other ports, you need to update them before moving to Azure.

Explanation

Your application has local or network IO operations.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, move persistent I/O to storage mounts (Azure Files/UNC). Keep local writes to temp only; connect to external dependencies via private endpoints/VNet to reduce latency.

IO operations outside of the application folder might not be available on Azure App Service. Possible solutions:
1. Files that the application needs can be deployed with the application or put in Azure Storage. You can use Azure Storage File Shares as a drop-in replacement for on-premises file share.
2. Other services that the application depends on might need to be migrated to Azure, this way you will get the benefit of lower latency in the cloud.
3. If your application needs to depend on services that run on-premise, you can connect your Azure and local networks with ExpressRoute, Hybrid Connections, or VPN solutions.

Explanation

Potential duplex communication is detected.

WebSockets work in most Azure environments and will not block migration. However, they need to be carefully reviewed to ensure the application will work correctly when it is scaled out.

Applications may require a communication backplane if broadcasting a message from one scaled out instance should also broadcast that message from other instances. Similarly, it may be necessary to enable session affinity if it’s required that users reconnect to the same server after a disconnect.

Similar issues could arise when server sent event streams are used (response content type "text/event-stream").

Data Storage & External Services

The website uses one SQL Server database through EF Core. An optional Azure Machine Learning scoring API supplies product recommendations; external OAuth providers can also be enabled through configuration. No message broker, remote cache, or separate application service was found in the target workspace.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • The website is a single deployable application with MVC, API, and SignalR entry points.
  • ICaldovaAssetManagerContext exposes EF Core data access to most controllers and query services.
  • Database schema deployment is represented by a separate ReadyRoll SQL project; the website maps to existing tables.

DTOs & Contracts

The API uses persistence model types (Product and Raincheck) directly for responses and the raincheck request body; no separate immutable API DTO or API-version contract was identified. Product contains a JSON-backed product-detail value that is materialized to a dictionary. MVC pages use view models such as ProductViewModel, ShoppingCartViewModel, and OrderDetailsViewModel. The active MVC JSON and SignalR configuration uses System.Text.Json, preserves property names, and ignores reference cycles; Newtonsoft.Json is used for model-level product-detail conversion. No protobuf or GraphQL schema was found.

Communication Patterns

  • Browser-to-website communication uses synchronous HTTP/HTTPS. Outside Development, the application enables HTTPS redirection and HSTS; TLS termination is deployment-host dependent.
  • The recommendation engine makes a synchronous HTTPS request to a configured Azure ML endpoint. Its HttpClient has a 30-second timeout; no application-level retry or circuit breaker is configured.
  • MVC checkout and admin operations use the local EF Core context. There are no separate business microservices, message brokers, or service-discovery clients.
  • External identity providers are optional and activated by configuration. The product and raincheck API controllers have no controller-level authorization attribute; checkout and order controllers require an authenticated user, while admin actions require the configured administrator role.
  • The database is configured through host settings. No API gateway or downstream response aggregation was identified.

Core Business Workflows

The application supports an online automotive-parts storefront with customer accounts, shopping carts, order checkout, store administration, and raincheck records. Catalog recommendations are an optional external enhancement to product browsing.

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships

CategoryCatalogGroups related productsContains Products
CartItemShopping CartProduct quantity in a visitor's cartReferences Product and cart identifier
OrderCheckout and OrdersCustomer purchase with shipping/contact information and totalContains OrderDetails; associated with a customer username
OrderDetailCheckout and OrdersProduct and quantity captured in an orderBelongs to an Order and references Product

Service-to-Domain Mapping

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
Caldova-Asset-Manager.WebsiteCatalog, Customer Accounts, Shopping Cart, Checkout, Store OperationsProduct, Category, CartItem, Order, OrderDetail, ApplicationUser, Raincheck, StoreShared SQL Server; optional Azure ML scoring endpoint; optional external login providers
Caldova-Asset-Manager.DatabaseShared persistence schemaTables for website entities and ASP.NET IdentitySQL Server deployment target

The application is a single deployable service. Its feature areas share one database and the website is the source of truth for catalog, cart, order, and raincheck records.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Browse and Search the Catalog

  1. A visitor opens the storefront or submits a product search.
  2. The MVC controller obtains products through the EF Core context or StringContainsProductSearch.
  3. The application renders product views; selected product results may be served from the in-process cache.
  4. If recommendations are enabled, the recommendation engine sends the product identifier to the configured HTTPS scoring endpoint and renders returned suggestions.

Workflow 2: Add Products and Place an Order

  1. A visitor adds a product to a session-associated cart; the website looks up the product and creates or increments its CartItem.
  2. The authenticated customer submits checkout details. Model validation runs before order creation.
  3. Checkout requires the configured promotional code FREE, case-insensitively; an invalid code returns the checkout view with an error.
  4. The website assigns the order to the signed-in user, creates order details from the cart, clears cart rows, and saves the order through EF Core.
  5. On order completion, the website checks that the requested order belongs to the current username before rendering its confirmation.

Workflow 3: Manage Catalog and Rainchecks

Administrators with the configured admin role can manage product catalog records through MVC actions. Raincheck API operations delegate to RaincheckQuery, which loads related Product, Category, and Store information and persists new raincheck records.

Cross-Service Data Flows

The only identified application-to-application data flow is the optional recommendation call: the website sends a model name and product identifier to the configured Azure ML endpoint and returns recommendation identifiers to the browser. The URI is required to be HTTPS and query values are URL escaped. No gateway aggregation, message-broker flow, or cross-service database access was found. If the recommendation request fails, the external call can fail the request; no circuit-breaker fallback was identified.

Business Workflow Sequence

sequenceDiagram participant Customer participant Website participant Checkout as "Checkout Controller" participant Cart as "Shopping Cart" participant Context as "EF Core Context" participant Database as "SQL Server" Customer->>Website: Submit checkout details Website->>Checkout: Bind order and validate model alt Invalid details or promotional code Checkout-->>Customer: Return checkout page with validation error else Valid details and code FREE Checkout->>Checkout: Set order username and order date Checkout->>Cart: Build order details from cart Cart->>Context: Add order details and remove cart rows Checkout->>Context: Add order and save changes Context->>Database: Persist order and details Database-->>Context: Save completed Context-->>Checkout: Order identifier Checkout-->>Customer: Redirect to order confirmation end

Business Rules & Decision Logic

  • Checkout requires an authenticated user and a valid order model; submitted username, order date, and total are controlled by server-side logic.
  • The promotional code is the literal FREE, compared without case sensitivity.
  • Order confirmation checks ownership by matching the order's username to the current identity.
  • The default calculator charges five currency units per cart item and applies a 6% tax rate, with 7.5% for postal codes beginning with 98.
  • Product recommendations are disabled by default and require externally configured endpoint, model, and API-key settings when enabled.
  • EF Core persists the order and related details in one SaveChangesAsync operation. No distributed transaction or saga is present.
  • Admin catalog operations use role-based authorization; no separate business audit trail was identified.

Data Architecture & Persistence Layer

The application persists catalog, cart, order, identity, and raincheck data in one SQL Server database through EF Core. The website maps to an existing schema, while a separate SQL project contains schema deployment artifacts.

Caching Strategy

Selected product data is cached in the process-wide MemoryCache.Default instance. Home page product lists use absolute 10-minute expiration; individual product entries use a 10-minute sliding expiration. Admin product updates invalidate selected product cache entries. The cache is local to each application process and is not distributed across instances; no cache-aside behavior is configured for the database context generally.

Data Ownership Boundaries

The website and schema project share one SQL Server database. There is no database-per-service or cross-service database access pattern. The optional recommendation integration sends product identifiers to Azure ML, but does not transfer database ownership or query another service's data store. Most application data access uses the ICaldovaAssetManagerContext abstraction.
